name: Agent-R: Training Language Model Agents to Reflect via Iterative Self-Training
authors: Siyu Yuan, Zehui Chen, Zhiheng Xi, Junjie Ye, Zhengyin Du, Jiecao Chen (Fudan University + ByteDance Seed; equal contribution Siyu Yuan & Zehui Chen)
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2501.11425, cs.AI; v1 submitted 20 Jan 2025, last revised 24 Mar 2025; not yet a peer-reviewed venue at time of writing)
reflection_type: learned-critic-model / search-guided: Agent-R trains the actor model itself to reflect and self-correct (revise) on the fly. Reflection-supervision data is generated via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and the actor model also acts as a model-guided critic that identifies the first erroneous step in a failed trajectory. The reflective ability is then baked into model weights via SFT (rather than verbal in-context critique a la Reflexion).
feedback_source: environment-reward (final reward r(tau) in [0,1] from the interactive environment determines good vs bad trajectories) combined with model-guided self-critique (the actor model identifies the first error step within its current capability). No human or expert/stronger-model supervision is used; the framework relies entirely on self-play. A small set of ten hand-designed revision-thought templates (rs) seeds the revision-signal text.
iteration_structure: tree/MCTS-search for data construction (k=8 rollouts per Monte Carlo estimation, max depth d=20) combined with iterative self-training: at each iteration the current actor model re-collects model-guided revision trajectories and is re-fine-tuned via SFT; reported over 3 iterations. Resulting agent performs mid-trajectory revision (episodic-style on-the-fly correction) at inference.
reflection_object: action trajectory (and the reasoning/revision step inserted into it). Agent-R constructs 'revision trajectories' that splice a failed (bad) trajectory up to the first error step with a correct (good) path sharing the same parent MCTS node, inserting a revision-thought token (rs) at the transition; the model learns to detect an erroneous action mid-trajectory and pivot onto a recovery path. Ultimately the corrective behavior is internalized into model weights via SFT.
requires_training: SFT (iterative supervised fine-tuning over multiple self-training iterations on self-generated revision + good + general trajectories; no PPO/DPO/RL is used by Agent-R itself, though DPO/contrastive baselines such as ETO are compared against).
reward_or_critic_model: verifiable reward (environment final reward in [0,1]) used to label good vs bad trajectories, plus self-as-judge: the actor model itself serves as a model-guided critic to locate the first error step within its current capability. No separately trained reward model or external stronger-model critic is used.
distillation_target: model-weights: the self-reflection / error-recovery capability is distilled into the agent's parameters via iterative SFT on MCTS-constructed revision trajectories (no external memory store, skill library, or prompt artifact is produced).
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered/scaffold-assisted but internalized into weights: reflection is not RL-emergent (no 'aha'-style emergence). It is engineered through an MCTS data-construction pipeline plus ten hand-designed revision-thought templates and a model-guided first-error-step detection mechanism, then trained into the model so the reflective/revision behavior becomes intrinsic at inference.
memory_type: none (no persistent external memory): Agent-R uses a within-episode interaction context/scratchpad for the agent trajectory; reflection knowledge is stored in model weights rather than in an episodic memory, skill library, or notes store. MCTS search trees are transient data-construction artifacts, not persistent agent memory.
memory_persistence: within-episode (the agent operates over one multi-turn trajectory at inference with no cross-episode external memory). Learned reflection capability persists in weights cross-task, but there is no explicit experience-memory module.
memory_curation_mechanism: n/a (no external memory to curate). For training-data construction, trajectories are selected via MCTS with reward thresholds that start low (to mitigate the cold-start problem) and are progressively raised across iterations; the good-trajectory mixture weight alpha is gradually increased so good trajectories converge toward optimal, but this is dataset curation, not agent-memory curation.
error_localization_granularity: step-level: the actor model identifies the FIRST erroneous action step within a failed trajectory, and revision/recovery is spliced in starting from that step (transition point t'). Agent-R explicitly contrasts this with a Direct-Revision baseline that only corrects at the terminal step (holistic/outcome-level).
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task at inference (the agent recovers from errors mid-trajectory within a single task episode), achieved via cross-task / multi-task training: revision trajectories from WebShop, ScienceWorld, and TextCraft are jointly trained (multi-task training found more effective than single-task in Finding 5).
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: mid-trajectory-recovery (correct in-flight): the central contribution is timely on-the-fly revision rather than waiting until the end of a rollout; the agent learns to detect the first error and pivot onto a correct path during the same episode, reducing dead loops.
task_domains: decision-making / interactive-agent tasks: web-navigation (online shopping), embodied/scientific text-game reasoning, and tool-use/crafting. All are multi-turn interactive environments with partial observation and delayed (terminal) reward.
benchmarks: WebShop, ScienceWorld (SciWorld), and TextCraft, all run on the AgentGym platform. Test sets: 200 tasks (WebShop), 200 (SciWorld), 100 (TextCraft).
headline_result: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Agent-R (iterative SFT on MCTS revision trajectories, 3 iterations) reaches an average score of 70.71 across WebShop/SciWorld/TextCraft (WebShop 63.91 reward, SciWorld 70.23 reward, TextCraft 78.00 success rate), versus 65.12 average for the strongest baseline ETO and 20.00 for the untrained Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, i.e. +5.59 points average over baseline methods and +50.71 over the base model.
baselines: Closed-source: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), Claude-3 (Haiku/Sonnet), DeepSeek-Chat. Open-source / trained agents: Llama2-Chat-13B, AgentLM-7B/13B (AgentTuning), Agent-FLAN, base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B w/ ETO (DPO contrastive), and Llama-3.1-8B w/ Direct-Revision (corrects only at trajectory end). Ablations: w/ Optimal trajectory, w/ Optimal+Good, w/ Optimal+ (GPT-4o-generated optimal).
gains_vs_baseline: Average +5.59 over the strongest comparable baseline ETO (70.71 vs 65.12); +8.35 over Direct-Revision (70.71 vs 62.36); +25.25 over GPT-4o (70.71 vs 45.46); +50.71 over base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (70.71 vs 20.00). In the revision/self-correction setting (Table 3, continuing failed trajectories), Agent-R reaches average 46.75 at iteration 3 vs 35.67 for Direct-Revision iter 3, 22.63 for GPT-4o, and 13.08 for ETO. Iterative gains for Agent-R: 39.92 (iter1) -> 42.62 (iter2) -> 46.75 (iter3).
compute_cost_profile: Training-heavy data construction: MCTS with k=8 rollouts per Monte Carlo estimation and max depth d=20 per simulation, run over 300 (WebShop)/200 (SciWorld)/200 (TextCraft) sampled tasks, plus 3 iterations of trajectory re-collection and SFT. Per iteration thousands of good and revision trajectories are produced (e.g. WebShop ~9000 good / ~2000 revision data per Table 1). Inference is a single multi-turn rollout (max 100 rounds in main eval, 50 in the revision setting) with no extra reward-model or external-critic calls, so inference cost is comparable to a standard fine-tuned agent rather than a multi-pass verbal-reflection loop. Exact GPU-hours / token counts are not reported in the main text.
known_limitations: Suffers from a cold-start problem in challenging environments (few optimal trajectories early), mitigated by low initial reward thresholds and mixing good + general (ShareGPT) data; good trajectories introduce noise (r(tau)<=1) and adding only good trajectories to optimal ones can decrease performance. The model-guided first-error detection is bounded by the actor's current capability. Evaluation is limited to three text-based interactive environments with a single 8B backbone (Llama-3.1-8B); no large-scale, multimodal, or real-world web (e.g. WebArena/SWE-bench) evaluation. The method requires environment-provided terminal rewards and many MCTS rollouts (costly). Generalization beyond the trained environments and to other base models is not extensively studied.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: env-reward: Agent-R depends on the interactive environment's final reward (r(tau) in [0,1]) to distinguish good vs bad trajectories during MCTS data construction. It does NOT use ground-truth step-level labels, human annotation, or a stronger expert model; the per-step error localization is done by the actor model itself (self-verify within current capability). So self-correction is driven by verifiable environment reward rather than oracle labels at test time.
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive: training on Agent-R revision trajectories yields consistent gains over base model, expert-trajectory SFT (AgentLM/Agent-FLAN), contrastive DPO (ETO), and Direct-Revision, and notably reduces dead-loop / repeated-action behavior (Finding 4) while shortening average revision length over iterations (Finding 3). The paper explicitly frames prompt-only intrinsic self-correction as ineffective/degrading and shows that weight-internalized, environment-reward-grounded revision works in interactive settings.
calibration_effect: not-measured (no explicit calibration/confidence analysis). The closest proxies are loop-avoidance (reduced repeated-action counts) and shorter average revision length, indicating better error detection rather than measured probability calibration.
failure_attribution_capability: attributes-failing-step: the actor model identifies the first erroneous action step in a failed trajectory (model-guided transition-point determination), which is a form of step-level failure localization used to construct revision data. It is not a general failure-mode taxonomy classifier or multi-agent responsibility attributor.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets error-loops / dead loops (agents repeating the same action sequence and getting stuck), cascading errors from uncorrected early mistakes, and the inability to recover from errors mid-trajectory (a form of superficial/absent self-reflection in expert-cloned agents). Maps to MAST-style modes such as error-loops and failure to recover; explicitly measures and reduces repeated-action-sequence counts.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new benchmark released; evaluation uses existing WebShop/ScienceWorld/TextCraft via AgentGym. Code, training scripts, and the MCTS-based revision-trajectory construction pipeline are released at https://github.com/bytedance/Agent-R (so the self-generated revision-trajectory data can be reproduced rather than being distributed as a fixed dataset).
builds_on: MCTS-based agent data generation and tree search for LLMs (e.g. AlphaZero-like/MCTS-for-LLM work); AgentGym interactive-environment platform (Xi et al.); AgentTuning/AgentLM (Zeng et al.) for behavior-cloning expert trajectories and mixing agent + general (ShareGPT) data; ETO (Exploration-based Trajectory Optimization, Song et al.) for contrastive good/bad trajectory training; Direct-Revision (terminal-step correction) baseline; and the broader self-correction literature (e.g. Huang et al. 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet', Kamoi et al. critical survey, CRITIC, SCoRe) which it positions itself against for interactive multi-turn settings.
extended_by_or_inspired: Cited/extended by subsequent agent self-training and step-level credit-assignment work, e.g. STeCa: Step-level Trajectory Calibration for LLM Agent Learning (2025), SPA-RL: Reinforcing LLM Agents via Stepwise Progress Attribution (2025), AgentRM: Enhancing Agent Generalization with Reward Modeling (2025), SAND: Boosting LLM Agents with Self-Taught Action Deliberation (2025), and Skill-SD: Skill-Conditioned Self-Distillation for Multi-turn LLM Agents (2026); also referenced in surveys on self-evolving agents and test-time compute / reasoning economy.
citation_count: 56 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; CorpusId 275757809). Google Scholar / NASA ADS list it under arXiv:2501.11425.
reasoning_model_native: No: Agent-R targets a standard (non-reasoning) instruction-tuned backbone (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and explicitly trains reflective/revision behavior into it, rather than relying on o1/R1-style models with built-in reflection. It is positioned as an alternative route to reflection for ordinary LLM agents; the paper notes that built-in self-correction is generally ineffective without such training.
on_policy_distillation_link: Strongly related: Agent-R is effectively an on-policy self-distillation / self-training loop. Revision trajectories are constructed from the current actor model's own rollouts (the first error step is identified 'within its current capability'), and SFT is performed iteratively on this self-generated data so the agent learns reflection 'based on its current policy' for better learning efficiency. This is closely aligned with on-policy distillation / skill-self-optimization ideas, though Agent-R uses SFT on spliced trajectories rather than KL-style on-policy distillation from a teacher.
sample_efficiency: Reaches reported gains in 3 self-training iterations; per environment MCTS is run on 300/200/200 sampled tasks with k=8 rollouts and depth 20. Iterative revision-setting scores improve 39.92 -> 42.62 -> 46.75 across iterations 1-3, with the largest jump from base model to iteration 1. The paper frames the model-guided, on-policy construction as yielding 'better learning efficiency' than direct-revision/expert data, but no formal sample-efficiency curve (#trials to a target) is reported.
